questions.text: Unstable or stable: the tachycardia algorithm and the shock

steps.bridge: Unstable means a shock. But this heart is still beating, so the shock has to be timed.

lesson.text:
Every fast rhythm you'll ever be shown starts with the same question, and it isn't what the rhythm is. It's whether the rhythm is hurting the patient.

Start with why a fast heart fails at all. The heart fills in diastole, and the coronary arteries fill in diastole too. As the rate climbs, systole hardly shortens, so it's diastole that gets squeezed. The ventricle fills less, so output falls. The muscle is fed less, at the very moment it's working hardest. You met those in the shock packets as filling and pump. A tachycardia attacks both.

So the algorithm lists five signs that this has happened. Hypotension. Acutely altered mental status. Signs of shock. Ischaemic chest discomfort. Acute heart failure. Three of them are low output, one is the starved coronary, and one is pressure backing up into the lung.

[[Unstable means hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure, caused by the rhythm. Any one of them means synchronised cardioversion.]]

If any one is present, the answer is electricity: a synchronised cardioversion. Why not a drug? Because a shock works in a single beat and doesn't depress the heart, while a drug takes minutes and most of them lower the pressure further. There's one permitted alternative. If the rhythm is regular and narrow, adenosine may be considered, because that rhythm is probably a circuit through the AV node and adenosine breaks it in seconds.

If none of the five is present, you have time. Take a twelve-lead ECG, secure IV access, and then measure the QRS. Under zero point one two seconds is narrow, which means the ventricles are being activated down the normal His-Purkinje wiring, so the rhythm starts above them. Zero point one two seconds or more is wide, and a wide tachycardia is VT until proved otherwise.

Now the way the bank asks it. The lowest score on this card, thirty per cent, was a man with recurrent palpitations, no chest pain, no breathlessness, and AF on the ECG. The tempting option was to sedate him and cardiovert at one hundred joules. He has symptoms, but none of the five signs. NEET's favourite wrong option here is the shock for a patient who is merely symptomatic. He's stable, and stable AF gets rate control with diltiazem or a beta-blocker.

The reverse error appears too. A pressure of seventy-five over forty, a rate of one hundred and eighty, a regular broad QRS: cardiovert. One Marrow key chose intubation for an unstable wide tachycardia, but only because cardioversion wasn't among the options. If it's offered, take it.

And one paediatric line, asked directly. A child's SVT converts with adenosine, returns within seconds, and now the child is unstable. More adenosine buys another thirty seconds. The answer is synchronised cardioversion at half to one joule per kilogram, then two joules per kilogram. Never verapamil or diltiazem in an infant, because they cause cardiovascular collapse.

So the first fork is settled: unstable, shock. But what makes this shock different from the one you give in an arrest?

steps.bridge: You know when the shock lands. Next, how much energy each rhythm needs under the current guideline.

lesson.text:
You've just chosen a shock for a heart that's still beating. That's the whole difference between cardioversion and defibrillation, and it comes down to timing.

Think about what a beating ventricle is doing through one cycle. At the R wave the whole ventricle has just been depolarised and is refractory. A shock landing there finds nothing excitable to disturb except the circuit you're trying to break. On the upslope of the T wave it's different. Some of the muscle has recovered and some hasn't. Excitable tissue lying beside refractory tissue is exactly the ground re-entry needs, and a shock that lands there can start VF. That's the R on T phenomenon.

So the machine is told to watch for the R wave and fire on its peak. That's synchronisation.

[[Cardioversion is synchronised to the peak of the R wave, so the shock can't fall on the T wave and cause VF. Defibrillation is unsynchronised, because VF and polymorphic VT have no reliable R wave to find.]]

Which rhythms get which follows from that. If there's an organised QRS, synchronise: VT with a pulse, AF, flutter. If there isn't, you can't. VF has no R wave at all, and polymorphic VT changes shape from beat to beat, so the machine may lock onto a T wave or never fire. Both are defibrillated.

The trap is simple: synchronised to the T wave, or to the P wave. It's the R wave. The T wave is precisely what you're avoiding.

So you know when the shock lands. Next, how big it should be.

steps.bridge: Timing and energy are set. Now the bedside: who is shocked at once, and what must be ready.

lesson.text:
The timing is fixed. Now the size of the shock, and here the twenty twenty-five guideline changed the numbers. That matters, because two bank keys still carry the old ones.

Start with why different rhythms need different energies. A shock ends an arrhythmia by depolarising enough muscle at once that the circuit has nowhere left to go. How much current that takes depends on how much tissue is involved. AF is many small wavelets wandering across both atria, so you have to capture a large mass of atrium in one go. Flutter is one large circuit in the atrium. A regular SVT is a small circuit through the node. Monomorphic VT is one organised ventricular circuit with a clean R wave.

The old teaching was to start low and climb. What changed is the evidence on starting low. Low-energy shocks failed more often, and worse, they sometimes provoked the next arrhythmia: VF when cardioverting AF, and AF when cardioverting flutter. A failed shock isn't free. It means another shock under sedation, more delay, and another chance of harm. Pooled biphasic trials found that two hundred joules gave over ninety per cent cumulative success, with no extra myocardial injury.

{{**AHA 2025, synchronised, biphasic**
AF | at least 200 J (class 2a)
Flutter | 200 J (class 2b)
Narrow regular SVT | 100 J
Monomorphic VT with a pulse | 100 J
Polymorphic VT | unsynchronised, defibrillation dose (class 1)}}

[[From twenty twenty-five, AF starts at two hundred joules or more and flutter at two hundred. Narrow regular SVT and monomorphic VT with a pulse start at one hundred. Sustained polymorphic VT is defibrillated, unsynchronised.]]

One point of honesty about the hundred. The guideline text gives a figure only for AF and flutter. The hundred joules for SVT and monomorphic VT comes from the algorithm chart, and it's what the keys use.

Now the traps. First, the old AF range. One grand test keys one hundred and twenty to two hundred joules for unstable AF, and a question bank item keys one hundred. In both, what's being tested is cardioversion over a drug, and that part is right. So pick cardioversion, and if two hundred or more is on the list, that's the current answer.

Second, polymorphic VT with a pulse. NEET's favourite wrong options are synchronised cardioversion at one hundred joules, and magnesium. The guideline treats every sustained polymorphic VT as unstable, whatever the QT, and gives an immediate unsynchronised shock. Magnesium belongs to one situation: torsades on a long QT that comes in runs and stops by itself. You'll meet it properly in the wide section.

You may see European numbers in a stem: maximum output for AF, seventy to one hundred and twenty joules for flutter and SVT, one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty for VT with a pulse. The bank keys follow the American numbers, so learn the box.

You've got the timing and the dose. What's left is the bedside: who gets shocked at once, and what you need around you.

steps.bridge: Now the whole section in one patient: fast AF, low pressure, wet lungs, duration unknown.

lesson.text:
Timing, energy, and now the doing of it. Four things on this card, and the questions come from three of them.

First, when to prepare to shock at once. The algorithm's number is a ventricular rate above one hundred and fifty. Why a rate? Because a reasonably healthy heart tolerates anything slower. If a patient is hypotensive at a rate of one hundred and twenty, the rhythm is very unlikely to be the cause. Something else is, sepsis or bleeding or hypoxia, and the heart is racing to compensate. Shocking a compensatory sinus tachycardia does nothing at all. So below about one hundred and fifty, look for the cause and treat that.

Second, what's at the bedside: a saturation monitor, suction, an IV line and intubation equipment. Each one answers a specific risk. Sedation can stop breathing or cause aspiration, and the shock itself can leave a bradycardia or VF.

Third, the prerequisites: consent, sedation and analgesia, and ruling out a left atrial clot. Take sedation first, because it was asked. The current guidance is that sedation is advisable in the awake patient, judged against how stable he is, and it must never dangerously delay the shock. The trap options are mandatory intubation, or an arterial line, before cardioversion. Neither is required, and both delay it.

Now the clot, which is the part asked most. In AF the atria don't contract, blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage, and after about forty-eight hours you must assume a clot has formed. Restore sinus rhythm and the atrium may throw it into the brain. So for AF of more than forty-eight hours, or of unknown duration, in a stable patient, you anticoagulate for three weeks first, or you look with a transoesophageal echo and cardiovert if the appendage is clear. Then comes the half people forget. After sinus rhythm returns on the ECG, the atrium is stunned and contracts poorly for weeks. New clot can still form.

[[Before elective cardioversion of AF beyond forty-eight hours: three weeks of anticoagulation, or a transoesophageal echo. After it: at least four weeks, whatever the stroke score, because the atrium stays stunned.]]

NEET's favourite wrong option is two or three weeks after. Three is the number before. Four is the number after, and seventy-eight per cent got it. Only then does the stroke score decide the long term.

And none of that applies to the unstable patient. Shock first, heparin alongside. The next card is exactly that patient.

Fourth, two procedural notes. Resynchronise after each shock, because many machines drop back to unsynchronised mode once they've fired. And if the machine can't find an R wave and the patient is crashing, don't wait: give an unsynchronised shock.

Now put the whole section into one patient.

steps.bridge: The unstable limb is done. From here the patient is stable, and the first rhythm is narrow and regular.

lesson.text:
Here's the section in a single stem. AF at one hundred and sixty. Pressure eighty-four over fifty. Basal crackles, saturation eighty-eight per cent. Duration unknown, not anticoagulated. Next step?

Run it the way you've just learned. Is the rhythm causing harm? At one hundred and sixty the ventricle has too little diastole to fill, and in AF the atrial kick that tops it up has gone. Output falls: that's the hypotension. Left atrial pressure rises behind a ventricle that can't fill, and that's the crackles and the falling saturation. Two of the five signs, and a rate above one hundred and fifty. He's unstable, and the rhythm is the reason.

So the answer is immediate synchronised cardioversion. The examiner has put three distractors in front of you, and each is something you'd rightly do for a different patient.

The first is rate control: IV diltiazem or metoprolol. Both are negative inotropes, and diltiazem dilates vessels as well. In a patient who's already hypotensive and wet, they can cause an arrest. On the mini test only forty-eight per cent chose the shock.

The second is the clot rule: heparin and delayed cardioversion, or a transoesophageal echo first. Duration unknown, not anticoagulated: it looks like the three-week patient from the last card. But those rules protect a stable patient from an elective procedure. In shock, waiting is the greater risk.

[[Unstable AF: shock now, with heparin started alongside. The three weeks and the transoesophageal echo are for the stable patient. They never delay an emergency cardioversion.]]

The third is amiodarone. A grand test gave new AF at one hundred and sixty-seven, five minutes after a thoracotomy, with a pressure of seventy-three over thirty-four, and offered a hundred and fifty milligrams of amiodarone. Still cardioversion, and eighty-seven per cent got it. Amiodarone is the stable patient's drug.

One harder version: the septic patient on the unit whose pressure falls to ninety over sixty as new AF begins at one hundred and fifty-five. In sepsis, AF is often a consequence and not the cause. But where the pressure drops with the onset of the rhythm, the keyed answer is cardioversion. And NEET twenty twenty-five asked it plainly: narrow, irregular, one hundred and forty, pressure eighty over fifty. Synchronised cardioversion. Diltiazem and metoprolol are for the stable patient, and digoxin is too slow.

The energy: two hundred joules or more for AF, synchronised. If the only cardioversion option says one hundred, take it anyway, because the decision is what's being marked.

That's the unstable limb finished. Everything from here is the stable patient, where you have time to ask which rhythm it is. Start with the tidiest one: narrow and regular.

spine: First question in any tachycardia: is the rhythm causing harm? Five signs: hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischaemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure.
Unstable → synchronised cardioversion (adenosine only if regular and narrow). Stable → 12-lead, IV access, then QRS: <0.12 s narrow, ≥0.12 s wide.
Synchronise on the R wave to avoid R-on-T. VF and polymorphic VT have no reliable R wave → unsynchronised shock.
AHA 2025: AF ≥200 J, flutter 200 J, narrow SVT 100 J, monomorphic VT 100 J. Older keys give 100 J or 120–200 J for AF.
Rate >150 before blaming the rhythm. Sedate the awake patient where stability allows; resynchronise after each shock.
Stable AF >48 h: 3 weeks of anticoagulation (or TOE) before, ≥4 weeks after. Unstable: shock now with heparin, no TOE.

open.text:
Patient C went home from the last packet with a scar on his heart. Two weeks later his monitor shows a heart rate of one hundred and eighty, and somebody asks you what to do.

Here's the thing NEET understands and most people forget. Before you name the rhythm, you ask a different question. Is this rhythm hurting him? A fast heart fails because diastole shortens first. The ventricles have less time to fill, and the coronary arteries have less time to fill too. So a fast rhythm can push a heart into the same failure you met in the Shock packets, filling and pump both falling at once.

[[Every fast or slow rhythm starts with one question: is it causing instability? If yes, electricity. If no, you have time to read it.]]

That gives the packet its shape. First, the decision itself: what counts as unstable, when to shock, and how much energy, with the twenty twenty-five numbers that NEET is starting to use. Then, once you have time, you read the complex. Narrow and regular: the supraventricular tachycardias, and adenosine. Irregular: atrial fibrillation and flutter. Wide: ventricular tachycardia, pre-excitation, and the inherited syndromes, including the Brugada question you missed in your grand test. And last, the slow rhythms: the blocks, atropine, and pacing.

Listen, all the way through, for the drugs that are banned in a particular rhythm. That's where NEET sets most of its traps.

Start with the question that comes before every rhythm. Is he stable?

questions.text: Narrow and regular: SVT, adenosine and the AV node

open.text:
The patient in front of you now is stable. That changes the question. You no longer ask how fast you can get rid of the rhythm. You ask where it's coming from, and the QRS has already told you half: narrow means it starts above the ventricles.

Take the tidiest case, narrow and regular. Almost everything in it hangs on one small piece of tissue. The AV node is the only electrical road from atria to ventricles, and it's slow by design. A regular narrow tachycardia at one hundred and eighty is nearly always a circuit that runs through that node. So block the node for a few seconds, and the circuit breaks.

[[A stable, regular, narrow tachycardia is usually a circuit through the AV node. Break it at the node, in order: vagal manoeuvre, adenosine, a longer-acting nodal blocker, and a shock only if all of that fails.]]

That's the ladder, and the cards climb it: the route, the drug, the patient, the fine print, and a quick sweep.

Listen for the trap on the first rung. Half the cohort went straight to adenosine. In a stable patient the vagal manoeuvre comes first.

Begin with the route.

steps.bridge: The second rung carries most of the weight. What is adenosine, and why push it so fast?

lesson.text:
Here's the route for the stable narrow tachycardia, and it forks once, on regularity.

Take regular first. A circuit that uses the AV node depends on the node conducting every single lap. Slow the node enough for one lap to fail, and the circuit dies. So each rung of the ladder is a stronger nodal block than the one before. First a vagal manoeuvre, because a surge of vagal tone slows the node and costs nothing. If that fails, adenosine, which blocks the node completely for a few seconds. If the rhythm survives or returns, a longer-acting blocker: a beta-blocker, or a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem or verapamil. And the current guideline states the top rung clearly: synchronised cardioversion for the unstable patient, and also for the stable one whose rhythm persists despite manoeuvres and drugs, or in whom they're contraindicated.

Now the other fork. If a narrow tachycardia is irregular, it isn't a nodal circuit. The two nodal circuits, AVNRT and AVRT, are always regular, because one loop goes round at one speed. Irregular means the atria are the source: AF, flutter with variable block, atrial tachycardia with variable block, or multifocal atrial tachycardia. The node isn't part of that circuit. It's only the gate the impulses pass through. So adenosine can't cure it, and the aim becomes rate control with a beta-blocker or a calcium channel blocker. That's the next section.

[[AVNRT and AVRT are always regular. An irregular narrow tachycardia is atrial, so adenosine has no therapeutic role and the treatment is rate control.]]

NEET's trap here is AVRT offered as a cause of an irregular narrow tachycardia. It never is.

Which regular rhythm is it? The commonest paroxysmal SVT is AVNRT, about sixty per cent, and women have it twice as often as men. So a young woman with no structural heart disease and a stable narrow tachycardia at one hundred and seventy has AVNRT, and sixty-seven per cent got that. If you're asked to rank all supraventricular tachycardias by frequency, it runs sinus tachycardia, then AF and flutter, then AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia and junctional.

Marrow sorts them by the P wave, and it's worth one pass.

{{**Narrow QRS, by the P wave**
More P than QRS | flutter or atrial tachycardia
1:1, RP <70 ms | typical AVNRT
1:1, short RP >70 ms | orthodromic AVRT
Long RP (RP > PR) | atypical AVNRT, PJRT, atrial tachycardia}}

The logic is distance. In AVNRT the circuit is inside the node, so atria and ventricles fire almost together and the P is buried. In AVRT the impulse has to travel down through the ventricle and back up a separate pathway, so the P arrives later.

And the order questions. Stable, narrow, one hundred and eighty: Valsalva, and only fifty per cent chose it. Vagal manoeuvre failed: adenosine, not cardioversion and not amiodarone.

So the second rung carries most of the weight. What is adenosine, and why is it given the way it is?

steps.bridge: Now put the ladder into one patient, and then change a single detail: asthma.

lesson.text:
The second rung of the ladder is a drug that lasts less time than this sentence.

Adenosine binds the A one receptor on the cells of the AV node and opens potassium channels. Potassium leaves, the cell hyperpolarises, and the node stops conducting. Then the drug is gone, because red cells and endothelium take it up so fast that its half-life is under ten seconds.

Everything on the card follows from that. It has to arrive at the heart as a bolus, so it's given as a rapid push into a large proximal vein, chased at once by a saline flush. Six milligrams first. If that fails, twelve.

[[Adenosine: six milligrams as a rapid push with a saline flush, then twelve. Its half-life is under ten seconds, so a slow injection is a wasted one.]]

What it converts is anything that needs the node for its circuit: AVNRT, AVRT, and many atrial tachycardias.

Its second use is diagnostic, and that's the version asked. If the node is only a bystander, blocking it doesn't stop the atria. The ventricles pause for a few seconds, and on the bare baseline you see what the atria were doing all along. A grand test gave six milligrams, a slowing of the rate, and saw-tooth waves at three hundred a minute: atrial flutter with two to one conduction. So the rule is this. If adenosine stops it, the node was in the circuit. If adenosine only slows it and it comes back, the rhythm is atrial.

Flutter at two to one is the one to suspect in advance. The atria run at about three hundred, every second beat gets through, and the ventricular rate sits at almost exactly one hundred and fifty.

The adverse effect on the card is severe bronchospasm in asthma. Adenosine receptors on mast cells and airway smooth muscle narrow an airway that's already twitchy. And most patients feel something: a flush, chest tightness, and a few seconds of dread. Warn them.

One limit, which you've met. When the tachycardia stops and then returns in seconds, giving more buys another half minute. In the unstable child, the answer was cardioversion.

Now put the ladder into a patient, and change one detail.

steps.bridge: Vagal manoeuvre and adenosine each hide fine print that the bank has asked.

lesson.text:
Regular, narrow, one hundred and eighty, no visible P waves, stable. You already know the first two answers, so say them quickly: a vagal manoeuvre, then adenosine six and twelve, and the card allows the twelve to be repeated once.

Now the detail that changes the answer. The patient is asthmatic.

Adenosine can trigger bronchospasm, so you reach the next rung by another route. Verapamil, or diltiazem, blocks the L-type calcium channel, and the AV node depends on calcium current for its upstroke, where the rest of the heart uses sodium. So the node is blocked just as surely, and the airway isn't touched.

[[SVT in an asthmatic: IV verapamil or diltiazem in place of adenosine. That is safe only with a normal ventricle and no pre-excitation.]]

This is the lowest score in the whole packet. On the mini test seven per cent chose verapamil. Adenosine is the reflex, and the reflex is wrong here. NEET's favourite wrong option is the default applied to the exception.

And hold on to the two conditions in that takeaway, because the next two sections are built on them. Verapamil weakens the ventricle, so it's wrong when the ejection fraction is low. And it blocks the node, which is dangerous when a second pathway exists beside it. You'll meet both.

Now the mechanism of the commonest cause. In some people the AV node has two ways through it: a fast pathway that recovers slowly, and a slow pathway that recovers quickly. Normally the fast one carries every beat. Then an early atrial beat arrives while the fast pathway is still refractory. It goes down the slow one, and by the time it reaches the bottom the fast pathway has recovered, so it climbs back up. Down the slow, up the fast, round and round. That's typical AVNRT.

Because the loop is inside the node, the impulse reaches atria and ventricles at nearly the same moment. So the retrograde P wave is hidden in the QRS, or shows at its tail: a small false S wave in the inferior leads, a small false r prime in V1. Where you can see it, it's inverted in leads two, three and aVF, because the atria are being activated from below.

That last line caught most people. A grand test showed a regular tachycardia at one hundred and eighty with inverted P waves in the inferior leads, and asked for the mechanism. Only forty-two per cent chose re-entry within the AV node. The wrong option was re-entry through an accessory pathway. That's AVRT, where the P sits clearly apart in the ST segment, and, if the pathway conducts forwards in sinus rhythm, a delta wave shows between attacks. The third mimic, atrial tachycardia, has a distinct P before each QRS and carries on regardless of the node.

The two steps you said quickly at the start each hide fine print that has been asked. That's the next card.

steps.bridge: One quick true-or-false sweep, and the narrow regular rhythm is done.

lesson.text:
You said vagal manoeuvre and adenosine in one breath. The bank has asked what's inside each.

Start with the manoeuvre, and why it works. Strain against a closed airway and the pressure in the chest rises, venous return falls, and the blood pressure drops. Let go, and blood surges back into the heart. The pressure overshoots, the baroreceptors fire, and the vagus slows the node. The surge on release is the useful part. So the modified Valsalva makes the surge bigger: strain at forty millimetres of mercury for fifteen seconds, sitting semi-recumbent, then be laid flat at once with the legs lifted to forty-five degrees. In the REVERT trial that converted forty-three per cent, against seventeen per cent for the standard manoeuvre.

Marrow asked it as a false statement: take a deep breath before straining. It's a sustained strain, not a breath in.

The alternative is carotid sinus massage, which presses on the baroreceptor directly. The rules are all about safety. Supine, on a continuous ECG, one side only, right side first, for five to ten seconds. Never both sides. And never where there's a carotid bruit, or a previous TIA or stroke, because your fingers can dislodge plaque.

[[Carotid sinus massage is contraindicated with a carotid bruit or a previous TIA or stroke. It is done on one side only, for five to ten seconds, on a monitor.]]

Now adenosine's fine print: when six milligrams is too much. Three situations. Through a central line, the bolus reaches the heart undiluted. After a heart transplant, the denervated heart is supersensitive to it. And with dipyridamole, which blocks the uptake that clears adenosine, or with carbamazepine, the effect is magnified. Marrow's key in each is three milligrams, and that's the exam answer: the only access is an internal jugular line, so the dose is three. The current American guideline goes further and says one milligram may be adequate through a central line or after a transplant. If an option says one and none says three, that's where it comes from.

[[Reduce the first dose of adenosine, to three milligrams on the exam, through a central line, after a heart transplant, or with dipyridamole or carbamazepine. Theophylline and caffeine block its receptor, so more may be needed.]]

In that other direction, theophylline and caffeine are adenosine receptor antagonists. The patient on either may need a larger dose.

One quick sweep, and the narrow regular rhythm is done.

steps.bridge: Two of those exceptions live in the irregular rhythm. Atrial fibrillation is next.

lesson.text:
This card is a sweep of nine true-or-false statements across the whole cardiology deck. Four belong to this packet, so take those and leave the rest for their own packets.

Adenosine is first-line for SVT in an asthmatic. False. Verapamil, as you've just seen.

Verapamil is fine for rate control in AF with an ejection fraction of thirty per cent. False. It weakens a weak ventricle. That's the next section.

Dabigatran is acceptable in rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF. False. Warfarin. Also the next section.

The maximum dose of atropine is three milligrams. True, at one milligram every three to five minutes, and you'll see why in the slow section.

The other five you'll answer when you get there. Peaked T waves are hyperkalaemia, not digoxin. After no shock advised, you resume compressions without a pulse check. Angiography two to twenty-four hours after successful lysis, which you did in the last packet. Resuscitation on ECMO is veno-arterial. And a normotensive pulmonary embolism is anticoagulated, not lysed.

Look at the pattern in the four, though. Every wrong statement takes a correct default and applies it to the exception.

[[Being stable lets you use a drug. The airway, the ventricle and the accessory pathway still decide which one: no adenosine in asthma, no verapamil with a low ejection fraction, no nodal blocker in pre-excited AF.]]

Two of those exceptions live in the irregular rhythm. That's where we go now.

spine: Stable regular narrow tachycardia = a circuit through the AV node. Ladder: vagal manoeuvre → adenosine → β-blocker or CCB → cardioversion if all fail.
AVNRT (~60% of PSVT, women 2:1): slow–fast loop inside the node, P hidden in the QRS or pseudo-r′ in V1. AVRT: P in the ST segment, RP >70 ms.
Adenosine 6 then 12 mg, rapid push + flush (t½ <10 s). Stops nodal circuits; unmasks flutter (saw-tooth ~300/min, ventricles ~150).
Reduce adenosine (Marrow 3 mg; AHA 2025 1 mg) via central line, after transplant, with dipyridamole or carbamazepine. Theophylline, caffeine blunt it.
Asthma → verapamil or diltiazem (normal LV, no pre-excitation). Carotid massage: one side, 5–10 s, never with a bruit or prior TIA/stroke.
Irregular narrow = AF, flutter or atrial tachycardia with variable block, MAT. Never AVNRT or AVRT; adenosine has no role.

open.text:
Narrow and regular was a circuit through the node, and you broke it at the node. Narrow and irregular is a different problem. The atria themselves are the source, firing chaotically at the same AV node.

So the node's role has changed. It's no longer part of the circuit. It's the filter that protects the ventricles. Slowing it doesn't cure anything, but it brings the ventricular rate down, and that's rate control. Two questions follow. Which drug slows the node in which patient? And since AF kills mostly through stroke, who gets which anticoagulant, and when is it safe to cardiovert?

[[In AF the node is the filter, not the circuit. Slow it with a beta-blocker or diltiazem, unless the ventricle is failing, the pressure is labile, or an accessory pathway bypasses the node.]]

Three exceptions, then. Listen hardest for the failing ventricle. There's a disputed key in this section: a patient with a low ejection fraction, AF and worsening breathlessness, keyed as beta-blocker, with thirty-nine per cent agreement. I'll show you what to mark.

Start with the card the bank asks most.

steps.bridge: The second exception in full: fast AF in a ventricle with an ejection fraction of thirty.

lesson.text:
This is the most-asked card in the packet, and it's one rule with three exceptions.

The rule first. In AF with a fast ventricular rate, too many atrial impulses are getting through the node. So you slow the node, with an IV beta-blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Diltiazem is a quarter of a milligram per kilogram over two minutes. Both also weaken contraction, and diltiazem dilates vessels too. The three exceptions are the patients in whom that matters.

{{**AF with a fast rate: the setting decides**
Stable, normal LV | IV β-blocker or diltiazem
Labile BP, post-op, septic | esmolol or IV amiodarone; not diltiazem
Decompensated low EF | amiodarone or digoxin; no IV β-blocker, no diltiazem or verapamil
Pre-excited | procainamide or ibutilide, shock if unstable; NO nodal blocker}}

Exception one, the labile pressure: the patient on the unit, septic or just out of theatre. Before any drug, correct what's driving the AF: potassium, magnesium, volume, the catecholamine dose. Then, if you need rate control, choose a drug you can switch off. Esmolol works in two to three minutes and has a half-life of about nine, because esterases in red cells break it down. A grand test asked for the fastest-onset titratable drug in post-operative AF with a labile pressure: esmolol. Diltiazem is the wrong choice here, because its vasodilation and negative inotropy add to a hypotension that's already there. The other good option is IV amiodarone, which slows the node with little fall in pressure or contractility. So for septic shock with new AF at one hundred and forty and a pressure of one hundred and two over sixty-five, the key is an IV beta-blocker, IV amiodarone is equally defensible, and the wrong options are diltiazem, and oral amiodarone, which is far too slow.

Exception two, the failing ventricle. With LV systolic dysfunction and decompensated heart failure, the card says avoid the calcium channel blockers and avoid IV beta-blockers. Both are class three, harm. Use amiodarone or digoxin. The next card is this patient. One version to bank now: septic shock, severe LV dysfunction, AF at one hundred and seventy, least suitable drug? Verapamil.

Exception three is the dangerous one. In pre-excited AF there's an accessory pathway beside the node, and it has no brake. Block the node and the atrial impulses take the pathway, at up to three hundred a minute, and the ventricle can fibrillate. So the card bans four: digoxin, beta-blockers, the non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and IV amiodarone.

[[Pre-excited AF: no digoxin, no beta-blocker, no verapamil or diltiazem, no IV amiodarone, and no adenosine. Shock it if unstable; procainamide or ibutilide if stable.]]

How do you recognise it? Irregular, wide, very fast, with QRS shapes that vary from beat to beat. A grand test gave an irregular wide rhythm at two hundred and eighty with varying complexes: AF with WPW.

One interaction, from Marrow. Never give IV verapamil or diltiazem soon after a beta-blocker. The nodal block and the negative inotropy add, and the result can be asystole. So diltiazem is contraindicated in all three: a low ejection fraction, after a beta-blocker, and pre-excited AF. And of the beta-blockers, carvedilol has no IV form.

Last line of the card. Converting AF or flutter beyond forty-eight hours without anticoagulation risks an embolus. If the AF is under forty-eight hours and you want sinus rhythm with a drug, the bank's drug is ibutilide: one milligram over ten minutes, repeated once. It converts flutter better than AF, roughly sixty to seventy-five per cent against thirty to fifty. It prolongs the QT and can cause torsades, so correct potassium and magnesium and monitor for at least four hours. Flecainide is only for a heart without structural disease; amiodarone where there is.

But notice the trap. One Marrow item keys ibutilide for stable symptomatic AF. The algorithm's answer for a stable irregular rhythm is rate control. Pick rate control if it's offered, and ibutilide only when the stem asks you to restore sinus rhythm.

Now the second exception in full: the weak ventricle.

steps.bridge: The rate is controlled. But in AF it's the clot, not the rate, that kills.

lesson.text:
AF with a fast rate again, but this time the ejection fraction is thirty per cent and the patient is in NYHA class four.

Go back to the pump from the shock packets. With an ejection fraction of thirty, output depends on whatever contractility is left. So the drug that slows the rate must not also weaken the muscle.

That rules out verapamil and diltiazem. They block the L-type calcium channel in the node, which you want, and in the working myocardium, which you don't. The European guidance advises against them once the ejection fraction is below forty. On the mini test only twenty-four per cent knew verapamil was wrong here.

What's safe? Three drugs, and the card puts a condition on the first. A beta-blocker, if the patient isn't decompensated. Digoxin. Amiodarone.

Here's why the condition matters. Over months, a beta-blocker is among the best drugs this patient will ever take. But given into a vein, into a ventricle that's wet and struggling today, its negative inotropy can tip him into cardiogenic shock. Digoxin slows the node by raising vagal tone, and it doesn't weaken contraction at all. Amiodarone slows the node with very little effect on contractility. So when the patient is congested, those two are the acute choice, with a diuretic for the congestion.

[[Low ejection fraction with fast AF: never verapamil or diltiazem. If decompensated, digoxin or amiodarone. A beta-blocker once the patient is compensated.]]

Now the disputed key. A patient with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction is admitted with AF at one hundred and thirty and worsening breathlessness, pressure one hundred and ten over seventy. The key says beta-blocker, and only thirty-nine per cent agreed. Worsening breathlessness is decompensation, and by the card an IV beta-blocker is avoided today. So how do you mark it? Read the options. If amiodarone or digoxin is offered for a patient who's clearly wet, that's the defensible answer. If the choice is only between a beta-blocker and a calcium channel blocker, the beta-blocker is what the examiner wants.

The drug that's contraindicated outright is dronedarone. It looks like a safer amiodarone, and it isn't. Two trials were stopped early for harm: ANDROMEDA, in recently decompensated severe heart failure, and PALLAS, in permanent AF. So no dronedarone in NYHA class four, after recent decompensation, or in permanent AF. Twelve per cent got that.

And a Marrow line worth a mark. Dobutamine speeds conduction through the AV node. Start it in a patient with AF and a low ejection fraction, and the ventricular rate can run away. What would have prevented it? Digoxin, given first.

You've controlled the rate. But the rate isn't what kills in AF.

steps.bridge: Outside the valvular group a score decides, and Marrow has asked what's in it.

lesson.text:
AF kills mostly through stroke. Three decisions on this card: which anticoagulant, when it's safe to cardiovert, and whether chasing sinus rhythm changes anything.

First the anticoagulant, and one group where the choice is fixed. In moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis, blood stagnates in a large left atrium. A mechanical valve adds a foreign surface. Those two are what's meant by valvular AF, and the drug is warfarin: an INR of two to three, or two point five to three point five for a mechanical mitral valve. The direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated. That isn't caution. It was tested. In mechanical valves, dabigatran caused more clots and more bleeding than warfarin, in the RE-ALIGN trial. In rheumatic heart disease with AF, rivaroxaban did worse than a vitamin K antagonist, in the INVICTUS trial. And aspirin is inadequate.

[[AF with moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis, or with a mechanical valve: warfarin, never a direct oral anticoagulant.]]

Only thirty-six per cent chose warfarin on the mini test. Keep the boundary sharp, though. A bioprosthetic valve, or other native valve disease, can have a direct oral anticoagulant.

Second, cardioversion in the stable patient with AF beyond forty-eight hours or of unknown duration. You have it already: three weeks of anticoagulation or a transoesophageal echo before, and four weeks after. One update. The twenty twenty-four European guideline has moved the line to twenty-four hours. The exam number, and the American one, is still forty-eight.

Third, rate against rhythm. It seems obvious that restoring sinus rhythm should prevent strokes. AFFIRM and RACE tested it, and it didn't. There was no difference in mortality, stroke or quality of life. Rate control's one advantage was fewer readmissions, because the rhythm-control patients kept coming back for cardioversions and drug toxicity.

Why didn't sinus rhythm protect them? Because most of the strokes happened in patients whose anticoagulation had been stopped or had fallen below range. They looked cured, and they weren't.

[[AFFIRM and RACE: rate control and rhythm control gave the same mortality and the same stroke rate, with fewer rehospitalisations on rate control. Anticoagulation decides stroke risk, not the rhythm.]]

Twenty-four per cent got that right. NEET's favourite wrong option is that rhythm control reduces stroke. For completeness, a later trial, EAST-AFNET four in twenty twenty, found that rhythm control started early, within a year of diagnosis, lowered cardiovascular events, which is why guidelines now offer it sooner. The exam answer remains AFFIRM.

So outside the valvular group, who gets anticoagulated? That's a score, and Marrow has asked what's in it.

steps.bridge: The narrow rhythms are done. Now the QRS widens, and a wrong drug can kill.

lesson.text:
Outside the valvular group, the decision to anticoagulate is a count of what makes a left atrial clot likely. The score is CHA2DS2-VASc, and the name is the list.

{{**CHA₂DS₂-VASc**
Congestive heart failure 1 | Hypertension 1
Age ≥75 **2** | Diabetes 1
Stroke, TIA or thromboembolism **2** | Vascular disease 1
Age 65–74 1 | Sex category, female 1}}

Don't recite it. Notice the two things that score double: an age of seventy-five or more, and a previous stroke, TIA or embolism. Those are the strongest predictors, which is why each carries a two in the name. Everything else is one point, and the maximum is nine.

The thresholds: anticoagulate at two or more in men and three or more in women, and consider it one point below that.

Why different numbers for men and women? Because the female point isn't an independent risk. A woman with no other factor is at low risk. Being female only magnifies the risk once another factor is there. So the threshold for women sits one higher, which cancels the point.

[[CHA2DS2-VASc: two points each for age seventy-five or more and for prior stroke or TIA, one for each of the rest. Female sex scores one, male sex scores nothing. Anticoagulate at two or more in men, three or more in women.]]

Marrow asked which factor the score doesn't include. Male sex. That's the trap, and it's an easy mark.

Since the sex point only ever cancelled out, the twenty twenty-four European guideline dropped it. Their score is CHA2DS2-VA: anticoagulate at two or more, consider at one, the same for everyone. Know that it exists. Answer with the older score unless the stem names the new one.

That's the irregular narrow rhythm: slow the node, respect the three exceptions, protect the brain. Now the QRS widens, and the stakes go up.

spine: AF: the node is the filter, not the circuit → rate control with an IV β-blocker or diltiazem (0.25 mg/kg over 2 min).
Labile BP (septic, post-op): esmolol (onset 2–3 min, t½ ~9 min) or IV amiodarone; not diltiazem. Never IV verapamil/diltiazem soon after a β-blocker.
Low EF: no verapamil/diltiazem; decompensated → digoxin or amiodarone, no IV β-blocker; no dronedarone in NYHA IV. Digoxin before dobutamine.
Pre-excited AF: no nodal blocker at all (digoxin, β-blocker, CCB, IV amiodarone, adenosine) → procainamide or ibutilide, or shock.
Rheumatic MS or mechanical valve → warfarin, never a DOAC. Others: CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women; male sex scores 0.
Stable AF >48 h: 3 weeks before or TOE, 4 weeks after. AFFIRM/RACE: rate = rhythm for death and stroke; rate control → fewer readmissions.

questions.text: Wide: VT, pre-excitation and the inherited syndromes

open.text:
So far every rhythm began above the ventricles. Now the QRS is wide, zero point one two seconds or more.

A wide QRS means the ventricles aren't being activated down the normal fast wiring. Either the impulse starts in the ventricle, which is VT, or it comes from above by an abnormal route: a blocked bundle branch or an accessory pathway. You can't always tell, so you decide by risk. In a patient with heart disease a regular wide tachycardia is VT about eight times in ten, and after an infarct more than nine. That's the scar from the last packet doing what you were warned it would do.

[[A wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proved otherwise. Treat it as VT: never verapamil or diltiazem.]]

The cards run from the stable wide route and its three drugs, to the accessory pathway, where the rules about the node turn upside down, to the inherited channel diseases. That card holds the question you missed in grand test seven, the survivor of a Brugada arrest.

Listen for one trap throughout: the right drug for an ordinary rhythm, given to the one patient it kills.

Start with the route.

steps.bridge: The drug is chosen. Now its dose, and the signs that tell you to stop.

lesson.text:
Stable, wide, and you're treating it as VT. The card has five lines, and two of them are prohibitions, which tells you where the danger is.

Start with the drugs you may use: procainamide, amiodarone or sotalol. What they share is that they act on ventricular muscle. Procainamide blocks sodium channels and slows conduction round the circuit. Amiodarone and sotalol block potassium channels and lengthen the refractory period, so the returning wavefront meets tissue that can't yet fire.

Which one? The ventricle decides. Procainamide and sotalol both weaken contraction and drop the pressure. So in heart failure or poor LV function the answer is amiodarone, and the bank has asked that twice: decompensated heart failure, stable monomorphic VT at one hundred and sixty, IV amiodarone. With a preserved ventricle, procainamide is the better drug. That comes from PROCAMIO, a small open-label trial of seventy-four patients with a stable regular wide tachycardia. Procainamide stopped sixty-seven per cent within forty minutes, against thirty-eight per cent for amiodarone, with major cardiac adverse events in nine per cent against forty-one.

[[Stable monomorphic VT: amiodarone when the ventricle is weak or failing, procainamide when LV function is preserved. Never verapamil or diltiazem.]]

Now the prohibitions. Verapamil and diltiazem must not be given for a wide tachycardia. If it's VT, they do nothing to the ventricular circuit. They just weaken the muscle and dilate the vessels, and the patient collapses. A grand test gave stable monomorphic VT in a heart failure patient already on metoprolol, and the wrong options were adenosine, verapamil and cardioversion. The answer was amiodarone, and about three in four got it. Verapamil is harm, adenosine doesn't treat VT, and cardioversion is for instability.

Adenosine has one narrow permission: when the wide rhythm is regular and monomorphic, as a treatment or as a test. The reasoning is that it might be SVT conducted with a bundle branch block. If so, adenosine ends it or shows you the atrial rhythm. If it's VT, a few seconds of nodal block usually does no harm.

And adenosine is forbidden in three settings: unstable, irregularly irregular, or polymorphic. Unstable needs a shock. Polymorphic can degenerate. And irregularly irregular with a wide QRS may be pre-excited AF, where blocking the node is the lethal move.

Where does electricity come in? For the unstable patient, at once. For the stable patient, when the drugs fail or can't be given. The trap is immediate cardioversion or defibrillation for a stable regular wide tachycardia. The keyed next step is an antiarrhythmic infusion.

One thing the bank assumes you can do is call it VT from the strip. Ischaemic heart disease, chest pain, wide QRS, no P waves, one hundred and fifty: VT, and over eighty per cent got that. The features that favour VT over SVT with aberrant conduction are AV dissociation, fusion and capture beats, a QRS wider than one hundred and sixty milliseconds, an extreme north-west axis, and concordance across the chest leads. AV dissociation is the one to understand: the atria carry on at their own slower rate, which proves the ventricle is driving itself.

You've chosen the drug. Now the dose, and when to stop.

steps.bridge: Every wide rhythm so far was regular. Now make it irregular and very fast.

lesson.text:
Three drugs, three doses, and each stopping rule or bar is the drug's own toxicity showing itself. Learn them that way and you won't have to memorise them separately.

Procainamide first. It's a class one A sodium channel blocker. You infuse it at twenty to fifty milligrams a minute, and you stop at whichever of four things comes first. The arrhythmia is suppressed: you've won. Hypotension appears: that's its vasodilating and negative inotropic effect. The QRS widens by more than half: that's the sodium block slowing conduction too far. Or you reach seventeen milligrams per kilogram. Maintenance is one to four milligrams a minute. Avoid it with a prolonged QT, because the drug and its metabolite lengthen repolarisation, and avoid it in heart failure.

Amiodarone. One hundred and fifty milligrams over ten minutes, repeated if the VT returns, then one milligram a minute for the first six hours. After that it's half a milligram a minute for the next eighteen. It blocks potassium, sodium and calcium channels and beta receptors, with little negative inotropy at these doses. That's why it's the drug for the poor ventricle.

Sotalol. One hundred milligrams, or one and a half milligrams per kilogram, over five minutes. Avoid it with a prolonged QT.

{{**Stable wide-QRS tachycardia, IV**
Procainamide | 20–50 mg/min; stop at suppression, hypotension, QRS +50% or 17 mg/kg; then 1–4 mg/min
Amiodarone | 150 mg over 10 min; then 1 mg/min for 6 h
Sotalol | 100 mg (1.5 mg/kg) over 5 min}}

Sotalol is the one that's been asked, in NEET twenty twenty-four: its adverse effect is due to what? It's a beta-blocker, so the tempting answers are bradycardia and hypotension. They happen. But sotalol is also a class three drug. It blocks the potassium channel that repolarises the ventricle, so the action potential lengthens and the QT with it, and a long QT is the ground torsades grows from.

[[Sotalol's serious adverse effect is QT prolongation and torsades, from potassium channel block. Procainamide and sotalol are both barred by a long QT.]]

So far every wide rhythm has been regular. Now make it irregular, and very fast.

steps.bridge: That was an extra wire. Next, normal wiring with a faulty channel, and your GT miss.

lesson.text:
The AV node has been your tool for two sections. Now see what it's for. It's a brake. It conducts slowly, and the faster it's driven the slower it conducts, which is called decremental conduction. That's what stands between an atrium fibrillating at four hundred or more and a ventricle that can't survive a fraction of that.

In Wolff-Parkinson-White there's a second connection between atrium and ventricle, a strand of ordinary muscle that bypasses the node. It has no brake.

In sinus rhythm you can see it on the ECG. The impulse goes down both routes. The pathway doesn't delay, so part of the ventricle is activated early: a short PR, under one hundred and twenty milliseconds. That early activation spreads slowly, through muscle and not through the fast wiring, so the upstroke of the QRS is slurred. That's the delta wave. Then the normal impulse arrives through the node and completes the job, so the QRS is a fusion of the two, and wide.

A grand test asked what lies behind a delta wave and a short PR, and only thirty-nine per cent chose an accessory AV pathway. The wrong option was a dual AV nodal pathway. That's AVNRT from the narrow section, and it leaves a normal ECG between attacks.

Now give this patient AF. Each atrial impulse has two routes. While the node is conducting, the beats it lets through also enter the pathway from its ventricular end and leave it refractory part of the time. Block the node, and that protection ends. The pathway carries the atrial impulses alone, at up to three hundred a minute, and that degenerates into VF.

[[In pre-excited AF, block the pathway, never the node. Unstable: cardioversion. Stable: procainamide or ibutilide.]]

So the banned list is every nodal blocker: adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers and digoxin. Verapamil and digoxin are doubly bad, because they also shorten the pathway's refractory period. And add one that isn't on this card: IV amiodarone. Its early effect in the vein is mostly on the node, and the American guidelines of twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-five class it as harm.

The treatment acts on the pathway itself. Procainamide or ibutilide slows it or lengthens its refractory period. If unstable, cardiovert. The cure is catheter ablation.

Here's a keying problem you should know about. Twice a grand test has asked which drug is contraindicated in WPW with fast AF, with verapamil as the key, while the other options included adenosine, esmolol and IV amiodarone. All of them are harmful. Agreement was forty-five to fifty-four per cent, because people who knew more hesitated. Mark verapamil. It's the classic answer.

Two discriminators. Pre-excited AF against VT: both are wide, but VT is regular with uniform complexes, and pre-excited AF is irregularly irregular with complexes that change width from beat to beat. And inside WPW itself, don't over-apply the ban. The common tachycardia in WPW is orthodromic AVRT: down the node, up the pathway, regular and narrow. The node is in that circuit, so vagal manoeuvres and adenosine are allowed. The ban is for the irregular, wide one.

Last, flecainide, the card's drug of choice from the mini test. It's a class one C sodium channel blocker, it slows conduction in the pathway, and it prevents AVRT. Two facts get asked. It's contraindicated in structural or ischaemic heart disease, because in the CAST trial it caused excess deaths after infarction. And its commonest dose-related non-cardiac effect is blurred vision. Marrow: blurred vision during treatment of paroxysmal SVT, which drug? Flecainide.

That was a heart with an extra wire. Next, hearts with normal wiring and a faulty channel.

steps.bridge: An ICD is for the arrhythmia with no removable cause. The next card sorts every indication.

lesson.text:
Two diseases on this card, and in both the heart looks normal on echo. The fault is in a channel. One is a disease of repolarisation, and one is a disease of the sodium channel.

Take torsades first. When the QT is long, the plateau of the action potential is prolonged. During a long plateau the L-type calcium channels have time to recover and reopen, and that produces a second small depolarisation before the cell has finished repolarising: an early after-depolarisation. If it reaches threshold it fires, and the result is a polymorphic VT whose axis twists round the baseline.

Magnesium suppresses those after-depolarisations, and it works even when the serum magnesium is normal. So the drug is magnesium sulphate, two grams IV. The American guideline grades it only as may be considered, yet it stays the exam answer. If the torsades keeps recurring, speed the heart up, by overdrive pacing at ninety to one hundred and ten or with isoprenaline. A faster rate shortens the QT and abolishes the pauses that set each run off. Keep the potassium high-normal. And if the patient is pulseless, defibrillate.

Now look at what you must not give: amiodarone, procainamide, sotalol. They're the three drugs from two cards ago, the right answer for ordinary VT. Every one of them prolongs repolarisation. Here they feed the arrhythmia.

[[Torsades on a long QT: magnesium two grams, a faster heart rate, and stop the QT-prolonging drug. Amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol make it worse.]]

A grand test made that the stem: a patient on IV amiodarone for AF has sudden syncope and torsades. IV magnesium, and ninety-one per cent got it. The mimic is polymorphic VT with a normal QT. That's usually ischaemia, magnesium doesn't help, and it's treated with amiodarone or a beta-blocker and urgent angiography.

Now Brugada, and slow down, because this is the question you missed.

The gene is SCN5A, a loss of function in the sodium channel. With less inward sodium current, the outward current that follows it dominates in the epicardium of the right ventricular outflow tract. The action potential there loses its dome, while the layers beneath keep theirs. That difference across the wall draws the ECG: in V1 and V2, a coved ST elevation of two millimetres or more, running down into a negative T wave.

Fifty-seven per cent knew the T wave is negative. The saddle-back shape with a positive T isn't diagnostic. The pattern can be hidden, and brought out by fever or by a sodium channel blocker such as ajmaline, flecainide or procainamide.

When does it kill? Whenever the sodium current falls further: at rest, in sleep when vagal tone is high, and with fever. So you treat fever aggressively. Its opposite is catecholaminergic polymorphic VT, a ryanodine receptor disease that kills on exertion, with a normal resting ECG.

Now the miss. Grand test seven, question one hundred and thirty: a patient with Brugada syndrome has survived a cardiac arrest. The tempting answer is a drug, and quinidine is the one usually offered. Reason it through. This patient has already shown that his substrate produces VF. The channel defect is permanent, so there's no cause you can remove. No drug has been shown to prevent death here. The only thing that reliably ends VF is a shock, so he needs to carry one.

[[Brugada syndrome with a survived cardiac arrest: ICD, class one. Quinidine is the adjunct, for a patient who refuses the device or keeps getting shocks. It is never the answer to what most reduces sudden death.]]

Marrow extends the ICD to arrhythmic syncope: Brugada with recurrent syncope, best therapy, ICD. Quinidine works by blocking that outward current, and isoprenaline is used acutely in an electrical storm. And the opposite case: polymorphic VT on levofloxacin and dofetilide. The cause is reversible, so stop the levofloxacin, hold the dofetilide until the QT normalises, and no ICD.

So an ICD is for the arrhythmia with no cause you can remove. That idea reaches well beyond Brugada.

steps.bridge: The fast side is finished. Now the monitor alarms for the opposite reason.

lesson.text:
You've just met one reason for an ICD. This card sorts all of them, and adds the other device. The trick is to keep two questions apart.

The first question is whether this patient has already had the event. If someone has survived a VF or VT arrest and there's no reversible cause, no acute infarct, no electrolyte or drug explanation, the substrate is still there and it will fire again. That's secondary prevention, and it's an ICD whatever the ejection fraction. Three trials, AVID, CIDS and CASH, compared the ICD with amiodarone. AVID showed a clear fall in mortality, the other two pointed the same way, and pooled together the ICD won. The Brugada survivor was this rule in a normal heart.

The bank's version: resuscitated out-of-hospital arrest, no infarct, ejection fraction thirty per cent, next step to reduce long-term mortality. Refer for an ICD, seventy-one per cent. NEET's favourite wrong option is amiodarone. Assessing the coronaries is part of the work-up, but it mustn't delay the decision.

The second question is for the patient who's had no event yet. That's primary prevention, and here the criteria are a list.

{{**Primary-prevention ICD**
LVEF ≤35%
NYHA II–III
On guideline therapy ≥3 months
More than 40 days after MI (90 after revascularisation)}}

Every item is a reason to wait or to exclude. Three months of therapy, because the ejection fraction often recovers on treatment and the patient no longer qualifies. Forty days after infarction, because two trials of early implantation, DINAMIT and IRIS, showed no fall in mortality: the early deaths are often not arrhythmic. And not NYHA class four, because those patients die of pump failure, unless they're also candidates for resynchronisation.

[[ICD: survivors of VF or VT arrest with no reversible cause get one whatever the ejection fraction. Primary prevention needs an ejection fraction of thirty-five or less, three months of therapy, and more than forty days after infarction.]]

Now the other device. Cardiac resynchronisation therapy treats a different fault. In left bundle branch block the septum contracts first and the lateral wall late, so the ventricle wastes work pushing blood from one wall to the other. Pace both ventricles together and they contract in step.

So what selects the patient? You'd think the echo would: look for the walls moving out of time. It was tried, and it failed. In PROSPECT the echo measures weren't reproducible, and in EchoCRT, patients with echo dyssynchrony but a narrow QRS got no benefit and possibly harm. The selector is the ECG.

[[CRT is selected by QRS width: left bundle branch block with a QRS of one hundred and fifty milliseconds or more, plus an ejection fraction of thirty-five or less. Not by echo dyssynchrony.]]

Twenty-six per cent got that. Between one hundred and thirty and one hundred and forty-nine milliseconds the benefit is weaker, and below one hundred and thirty there's none.

That's the fast side of the monitor complete. Turn to the patient whose alarm is ringing for the opposite reason.

spine: Wide-complex tachycardia = VT until proved otherwise (~80% with heart disease, >90% after MI). Never verapamil or diltiazem.
Stable VT: amiodarone if the LV is poor or failing; procainamide if preserved (PROCAMIO). Adenosine only if regular and monomorphic.
Procainamide 20–50 mg/min to suppression, hypotension, QRS +50% or 17 mg/kg. Amiodarone 150 mg/10 min then 1 mg/min. Sotalol 100 mg/5 min: QT, torsades.
WPW: short PR, delta wave. Pre-excited AF (irregular, wide, up to 300/min): no nodal blocker, no IV amiodarone → procainamide or ibutilide, or shock.
Torsades: Mg 2 g, pace or isoprenaline, stop QT drugs. Brugada: SCN5A, coved ST + negative T in V1–V2, dies at rest, sleep, fever → ICD after arrest (class I) or arrhythmic syncope.
ICD: arrest survivor with no reversible cause, any EF. Primary: EF ≤35%, 3 months of therapy, >40 days post-MI. CRT: LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, not echo.

questions.text: Slow: sinus and junctional, the blocks, and pacing

open.text:
Now the heart is too slow, and the thinking is simpler, because a slow rhythm is always one of two failures. Either the pacemaker isn't firing, or it's firing and the impulse isn't getting through.

The sinus node fires, the impulse crosses the atria, passes the AV node, runs down the bundle of His and out through the Purkinje fibres. A fault at the top is sinus node trouble. A fault in the middle or below is AV block. And for AV block one question decides everything: is the block in the node, or below it?

[[In a slow rhythm, find the level. A block in the AV node is vagal, usually benign, and answers to atropine. A block below the node is unstable, ignores atropine, and needs pacing.]]

The reason is anatomy. The vagus supplies the sinus node and the AV node, and almost nothing beneath them. Atropine only removes the vagus.

The cards run from the top down: the rhythms, the blocks, the algorithm, and two patients.

The trap to listen for is atropine given to an infranodal block. The scores there fell to twenty-two and forty-three per cent, and one key is wrong.

Start at the top.

steps.bridge: That was failure at the top. Now the impulse has to cross from atrium to ventricle.

lesson.text:
Start with the pacemaker itself. Bradycardia is a rate below sixty, and it may be perfectly normal.

In sinus bradycardia the node is firing slowly, and nothing else is wrong. Every P wave is a sinus P, each one conducts, and the PR interval is normal. An athlete or a sleeping patient has it from vagal tone. Drugs cause it. And the card lists the pathological causes: hypoxia, infarction, raised intracranial pressure and hypothyroidism. Each has a reason. Inferior infarction, because the right coronary usually feeds the node, and the inferior wall triggers a vagal reflex. Raised intracranial pressure, through the Cushing reflex. You treat it only when it causes symptoms. The bank's version is easy: elderly, syncope, a regular rhythm at forty with normal P and QRS. Sinus bradycardia, ninety-two per cent.

Now suppose the sinus node fails altogether, or its impulse can't get out. The heart has a reserve. The AV junction will fire by itself at forty to sixty a minute. That's a junctional escape rhythm, and you recognise it from two things. The impulse spreads down the normal wiring, so the QRS is narrow. And it spreads backwards into the atria, so the P wave is inverted in the inferior leads, and depending on timing it comes just before the QRS, hides inside it, or follows it.

[[A normal P before every QRS with a normal PR is sinus bradycardia. An inverted, absent or late P with a narrow QRS is a junctional rhythm, which means the sinus node has failed above it.]]

The card's causes for a junctional rhythm are hyperkalaemia, sino-atrial exit block and severe sinus bradycardia. Treat the cause if there are symptoms.

That middle one has been asked, and no card explains it, so here it is. In sino-atrial exit block the node fires on time, but the impulse fails to leave the node and reach the atrium. You can't see the node fire on a surface ECG. You only see the missing P wave. So how do you tell it from a node that simply paused?

By arithmetic. If the node kept its rhythm and one impulse was blocked, the gap is exactly two of the normal P to P intervals. That's type two exit block: a constant P to P interval, then a sudden pause that's an exact multiple of it. A sinus pause or arrest has no fixed relation to the cycle, because the node itself stopped. And type one is the Wenckebach version: the P to P intervals shorten progressively, then a pause that's less than two cycles.

[[Sino-atrial exit block type two: a constant P to P interval, then a pause that is an exact multiple of it, usually double. A sinus pause bears no fixed relation to the P to P interval.]]

NEET's wrong option for the constant rhythm with a pause of exactly two cycles is sinus arrest. It's exit block, type two, and seventy-five per cent got it.

So that's failure at the top. Now the impulse leaves the atrium and has to cross to the ventricle.

steps.bridge: You can read the slow rhythm and find its level. Now treat it.

lesson.text:
The impulse has left the atria. Between it and the ventricles lie the AV node, then the bundle of His and its branches. The four blocks on this card are really two diseases: a tired node, and broken wiring below it.

First degree is hardly a block at all. Every P conducts, one to one, just slowly: a PR above two hundred milliseconds. It can be normal, or come from drugs, an inferior infarct or myocarditis. It usually needs no treatment. One item gave an asymptomatic patient with first-degree block, and only thirty-nine per cent chose discharge. Don't admit a long PR.

Second degree means some P waves don't get through, and there are two kinds.

Mobitz one, or Wenckebach, is the AV node tiring. The node conducts decrementally, so each beat finds it a little less recovered, and the PR lengthens beat by beat until one P fails. The node rests, and the cycle begins again. Progressive PR lengthening, then a dropped QRS: NEET twenty twenty-five asked exactly that. Because the fault is in the node, the QRS is usually narrow, and the node listens to the vagus.

Mobitz two is the wiring below. The His-Purkinje system doesn't tire gradually. It conducts fully or not at all. So the PR is fixed, and then without warning a QRS is missing. The QRS is often wide, because the bundle branches are diseased, and the next step can be complete block with nothing reliable underneath. So Mobitz two necessitates treatment: a cardiologist and transvenous pacing.

Now the test that separates them, which Marrow and the grand tests both ask. Atropine and exercise speed up conduction in the node. So they improve Mobitz one. In Mobitz two they can't help the diseased wiring, but they do speed up the sinus rate, so more impulses arrive at a system that can only pass so many, and the block gets worse. Carotid massage does the reverse on both.

{{**Nodal vs infranodal block**
Feature | Nodal (Mobitz I) | Infranodal (Mobitz II)
QRS | narrow | often wide
Atropine, exercise | improve | worsen or no effect
Carotid massage | worsens | may improve
Infarct | inferior | anterior
Course | benign | progresses; pace}}

[[Atropine and exercise improve a nodal block and worsen an infranodal one. Mobitz one is nodal, narrow and usually benign. Mobitz two is infranodal, often wide, and needs pacing.]]

Marrow's form: which feature is not seen in type one block? Worsening with atropine.

Complete heart block is no relationship between P and QRS: the P to P interval is constant, the R to R interval is constant, and they're independent. Look at the escape rhythm to find the level. Narrow, at forty to sixty, is a junctional pacemaker beneath a nodal block. Wide and slow, at twenty to forty, is ventricular and unreliable. Asymptomatic: pacer pads on, monitor, admit. Symptomatic: pace.

And the card's last line: some blocks can't be classified. In two to one block every second P is dropped, so there are never two conducted beats in a row to compare, and you can't say whether the PR was lengthening. Use the company it keeps. A narrow QRS in a vagal setting means the node. The stem was a sleeping athlete with two to one block, and only forty-two per cent chose the AV node; the wrong options were the His bundle and the bundle branches. A wide QRS, or an anterior infarct, means below the node.

Now the wrong key I promised. One item gives an anterior infarct with second-degree block and keys it as Mobitz one, benign, give atropine. That's wrong. The left anterior descending artery supplies the His-Purkinje system, so block after an anterior infarct is infranodal and needs transvenous pacing. The inferior infarct is the one with the benign nodal block. On the day, choose the option that puts the block in the His bundle or Purkinje fibres, and paces.

You can read the slow rhythm. Now treat it.
