lesson.text:
The bradycardia algorithm opens with the same question as the tachycardia one. Is the rhythm causing harm? And it uses the same five signs: hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure. The current guideline adds that the rate is typically below fifty before the rhythm can be blamed.

If none is present, monitor and observe, and look for the cause.

If one is, atropine. It blocks the muscarinic receptor, which takes the vagus off the sinus node and the AV node. One milligram as a bolus, repeated every three to five minutes, to a maximum of three milligrams. Why three? Because that's complete vagal blockade. Beyond it there's no vagus left to block.

[[Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine one milligram every three to five minutes, maximum three. If it fails: transcutaneous pacing, or dopamine, or adrenaline. If those fail: transvenous pacing.]]

If atropine fails, the algorithm offers three things as equals: transcutaneous pacing, a dopamine infusion, or an adrenaline infusion. Pacing goes round the conduction problem altogether. The two infusions stimulate the beta one receptor, so the rate rises whatever the vagus is doing. And if those fail, transvenous pacing and an expert, which the current guideline calls reasonable for unstable bradycardia that's refractory to drugs.

That's the route. Now the four places the bank bends it.

One, the dose. A Marrow key says atropine nought point five milligrams. That was the American dose before twenty twenty, and it's still the European dose, so it isn't wrong. The current American dose is one milligram. If one is offered, pick one.

Two, the second-line drug. NEET twenty twenty-five asked what follows when pacing fails, and keyed dopamine. A grand test gave pericarditis after bypass surgery, a rate of thirty-three, three milligrams of atropine already given, and pacing on its way. The wrong options were more atropine, norepinephrine and isoproterenol. The answer was dopamine, and thirty-five per cent got it. More atropine is pointless after three milligrams, and norepinephrine adds afterload with little effect on rate. So for the exam: dopamine if it's offered, adrenaline if it isn't. The European algorithm uses isoprenaline or adrenaline, which is why isoprenaline appears as a distractor.

Three, and this is the big one: atropine in an infranodal block. You know from the last card that atropine does nothing below the node and can worsen the block. So in unstable Mobitz two, or complete heart block with a wide escape, pacing mustn't wait for atropine to fail. A grand test gave a septic patient, pressure seventy-five over forty, Mobitz two: transcutaneous pacing, and forty-three per cent chose it. Another gave a rate of twenty-eight, confusion, wide-complex Mobitz two, atropine already failed: transcutaneous pacing.

But be ready for the key that goes the other way. A septic patient, rate thirty-four, complete heart block, pressure eighty over fifty, with atropine keyed as the first step and only twenty-two per cent agreeing. The algorithm does begin with atropine, and that's the letter of it; you'd still prepare the pacer at once. The tempting wrong answer there was a permanent pacemaker, which comes after stabilisation. So: atropine as the first step where the stem doesn't tell you the level, pacing where it tells you the block is infranodal.

Four, the easy ones. A rate of forty-two after an acute coronary syndrome and a stent, first drug: atropine. Mobitz one with a pressure of eighty over sixty: atropine one milligram. Unstable sinus bradycardia with pauses: atropine, and arrange temporary pacing.

The two infusions have doses, and their units are a trap.

steps.bridge: The third option on that rung was electricity through the chest wall.

lesson.text:
Two infusions, and the only thing to learn is that their units differ.

Dopamine is dosed by weight: five to twenty micrograms per kilogram per minute. At that dose it drives the beta one receptor, raising rate and contractility, and towards the top of the range it adds alpha vasoconstriction. Titrate to the response, and taper it slowly, because stopping it suddenly can drop the pressure.

Adrenaline is a flat adult rate: two to ten micrograms per minute. No kilograms.

[[Bradycardia infusions: dopamine five to twenty micrograms per kilogram per minute. Adrenaline two to ten micrograms per minute, with no per kilogram.]]

The trap is adrenaline at two to ten micrograms per kilogram per minute. In a seventy-kilogram adult that's seventy times the dose. On the mini test only thirty-four per cent picked the right units.

The third option at that rung was electricity through the chest wall.

steps.bridge: While the pads go on, ask why the heart slowed in the first place.

lesson.text:
Transcutaneous pacing drives the heart through the chest wall, and it's a bridge: to a transvenous wire, or to the cause being fixed. Its indication is the haemodynamically unstable bradycardia.

Four practical points, each with a reason. Give sedation and analgesia, with an opioid or a benzodiazepine, and obtain consent, because the current contracts the chest wall muscles and it hurts. Place the pads as the device shows. Set the rate at sixty to eighty: enough to restore output without loading a heart that may be ischaemic. And for the current, turn it up until every spike captures, then set it two milliamps above that, because the threshold drifts and you want a margin.

Now the point that matters more than the numbers. Capture on the monitor is electrical: a wide QRS and a broad T wave after each spike. That tells you the muscle depolarised. It doesn't tell you it pumped. You confirm mechanical capture with a pulse, and you feel for it at the femoral artery or read it off an arterial line, because at the neck the twitching muscles can fool your fingers.

[[Transcutaneous pacing: sixty to eighty a minute, current two milliamps above the capture threshold, with sedation. Capture is confirmed by a femoral pulse or an arterial trace, not by the monitor.]]

And one line from the grand tests. Pacing is for bradycardia with a pulse. The current guideline states that routine pacing isn't recommended in established cardiac arrest, asystole or pulseless electrical activity, whatever the timing, because it doesn't improve return of circulation or survival.

While the pads go on, ask why the heart slowed in the first place.

steps.bridge: Two patients to close. The first: slow sinus rhythm, low pressure.

lesson.text:
While you give atropine and set up the pacer, you look for the cause, at the same time and not afterwards, because all four of the card's categories are reversible.

Ischaemia or infarction. You know the two patterns now: the inferior infarct with a vagal, nodal bradycardia, and the anterior infarct with block below the node.

Drugs and toxins: calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and digoxin. All three slow the node, and their effects add. Marrow asked it neatly: a patient on metoprolol for AF develops symptomatic bradycardia, and which other drug is the synergistic culprit? Digoxin. It slows the node through the vagus, on top of the beta-blocker.

[[Bradycardia has four reversible causes to look for at once: ischaemia, drugs such as calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers and digoxin, hypoxia, and electrolytes, above all hyperkalaemia.]]

Hypoxia. It's a late and ominous cause, and in a child it's the usual one. Hold that thought for two cards.

And electrolytes, chiefly hyperkalaemia, which depolarises cells and slows conduction at every level. Calcium protects the membrane while you bring the potassium down.

Each of the poisonings has its own antidote, and atropine isn't it. That's the whole of the next packet, so I'll leave it there.

Now two patients to close the section. The first has a slow sinus rhythm and a low pressure.

steps.bridge: The last card: the block atropine can't reach, and a child who isn't a small adult.

lesson.text:
A rate of thirty-six, pressure seventy-six over forty, confused. The strip shows sinus bradycardia with no high-grade block.

You can answer this in one line now. Atropine one milligram, every three to five minutes, to three milligrams. Then dopamine at five to twenty micrograms per kilogram per minute, or adrenaline at two to ten micrograms per minute, or transcutaneous pacing. And while the pacer's being set up, start an infusion.

So use this card for the question underneath: why is atropine first at all? Only because most symptomatic bradycardia is vagal and sits at or above the node. Atropine is a bet on that. When it fails, it has told you something: the problem isn't vagal, so the next step either drives the beta receptor directly or bypasses conduction.

One detail on the dose. Less than half a milligram can slow the heart further, a paradoxical effect, which is one reason the dose isn't given timidly.

The card ends by asking when the bet is lost before you place it. Two situations.

The first you know: block below the node. Mobitz two, or complete heart block with a wide escape. The His-Purkinje system has almost no vagal supply.

The second is the transplanted heart. The surgeon cuts the nerves, and a denervated heart has no vagal tone to remove. So atropine does nothing, and neither does glycopyrrolate. Ephedrine fails too, because it works largely by releasing noradrenaline from nerve endings that are no longer there. Atropine can even provoke high-grade block in these patients. What works is a drug that acts directly on the receptor, isoprenaline or adrenaline, or pacing.

[[Atropine is useless in infranodal block and in the transplanted, denervated heart. After a transplant use a direct-acting drug, isoprenaline or adrenaline, or pace.]]

Marrow: heart transplant three years ago, bradycardia during an operation, best drug? Isoprenaline. Notice the symmetry with the narrow section. The same denervated heart that ignores atropine is supersensitive to adenosine.

One more transplant fact, from both banks. Up to half of patients have sinus node dysfunction early after an orthotopic transplant, mainly from surgical trauma or ischaemia to the donor's node. It usually resolves within weeks to three months. You support the rate at ninety to one hundred and ten, with atrial pacing through the epicardial wires or with isoprenaline, and a permanent pacemaker is only for those in whom it persists.

The second patient has the block that atropine can't reach.

Three pacing decisions to finish, and the first two are the level of the block again.

Mobitz two with syncope and no reversible cause. It's disease of the His-Purkinje system, it progresses without warning to complete block, and what's left underneath is a slow, unreliable ventricular escape. Once you've excluded drugs, ischaemia and hyperkalaemia: a permanent pacemaker.

Complete heart block with shock. Pace. But in what order? Transcutaneous now, transvenous next, with a chronotrope as a bridge. This is the forty-three per cent question again: a septic patient with syncope, Mobitz two on the strip, pressure seventy-five over forty, initial intervention. NEET's favourite wrong option is the transvenous pacemaker, which is the better pacemaker and takes time to place. The pads take a minute. Atropine works on the node, not below it. And dobutamine isn't the rescue.

[[Unstable infranodal block: transcutaneous pacing first, as the bridge to a transvenous wire. Symptomatic Mobitz two with no reversible cause ends in a permanent pacemaker.]]

The third decision is a child, and the adult algorithm doesn't apply. A rate of forty-six, poor perfusion, and oxygenation and ventilation are already good.

In an adult, bradycardia is usually a conduction problem. In a child it's usually the last stage of hypoxia: the heart slowing because it's running out of oxygen, on its way to stopping. So the first move is always to oxygenate and ventilate. This stem tells you that's been done, and the rate is still below sixty with poor perfusion. A child's output depends heavily on rate. So this is treated as an arrest that's about to happen.

[[A child with a heart rate below sixty and poor perfusion despite good oxygenation and ventilation: start CPR and give adrenaline, nought point nought one milligrams per kilogram.]]

That's nought point one millilitres per kilogram of the nought point one milligram per millilitre solution, by vein or into bone, to a maximum of one milligram. Only twenty-two per cent got this. The wrong options are atropine and dopamine, the adult reflexes. Atropine, at nought point nought two milligrams per kilogram, is kept for raised vagal tone or a primary AV block.

That's the rhythm packet. Fast or slow, you asked the same thing first: is the rhythm causing harm? If it was, electricity. If it wasn't, you found the level, the atrium, the node, a pathway or the ventricle, and chose the drug that acts there.

But look back at how often the cause was something the patient had been given. Digoxin with a beta-blocker behind a bradycardia. Verapamil for the wrong rhythm. A long QT from two prescriptions. And in this last section you met hearts that atropine can't fix. Every drug in this packet treats a rhythm at one dose and causes one at another. So that's next: the cardiac drugs themselves, and what you do for the heart that's been poisoned by them.

spine: A slow rhythm is one of two failures: the pacemaker isn't firing (sinus node) or the impulse isn't conducted (AV block). Find the level.
Sinus bradycardia: normal P and PR. Junctional escape: narrow QRS, P inverted, absent or after the QRS. SA exit block type II: pause = exact multiple of PP.
Nodal block (Mobitz I, inferior MI, narrow QRS): atropine and exercise improve it. Infranodal (Mobitz II, anterior MI, wide QRS): they worsen it → pace.
Algorithm: atropine 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg → TCP or dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min or adrenaline 2–10 mcg/min → transvenous pacing.
TCP: 60–80/min, 2 mA above capture, confirm with a femoral pulse. No routine pacing in established arrest.
Atropine fails in infranodal block and the transplanted heart (isoprenaline). Child HR <60 + poor perfusion despite O₂ and ventilation → CPR + adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg.

close.text:
So let's walk back through it, rhythm by rhythm.

You began by asking whether the rhythm was hurting him. If it was, you shocked, synchronised, with the right energy. If it wasn't, you read the complex. Narrow and regular sent you to vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine. Irregular sent you to rate or rhythm, and to anticoagulation. Wide sent you to ventricular tachycardia until proven otherwise, and to the drugs you must never give. And slow sent you to atropine, then to pacing while you looked for the cause.

Now the traps.

One. Unstable atrial fibrillation. The tempting energy is one hundred joules. Twenty twenty-five starts atrial fibrillation at two hundred joules or more. One hundred is for the narrow regular rhythms.

Two. A stable narrow tachycardia at one hundred and eighty. The tempting first step is adenosine. It's the vagal manoeuvre first, the modified Valsalva, and adenosine when that fails.

Three. Atrial fibrillation in Wolff–Parkinson–White. The tempting answer is that only verapamil is banned. [[In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, every AV nodal blocker is harmful: adenosine, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, and intravenous amiodarone.]] Cardiovert, or use procainamide.

Four. A survivor of a Brugada arrest. The tempting answer is quinidine. [[After a survived arrest in Brugada syndrome, the answer is an ICD, class one.]] You missed this one.

Five. Torsades. The tempting drug is amiodarone, because it treats ventricular tachycardia. But amiodarone prolongs the QT. Magnesium is the answer, and you stop the drug that caused it.

And six. Unstable Mobitz two. The tempting first step is atropine. The block sits below the node, so atropine won't help much. Pace, transcutaneously, as the bridge.

The check comes up on the next screen. Answer each in your head before you tap it open.

And notice how many of those traps were drugs. The same drug that treats a rhythm at one dose causes one at another. So next, the drugs themselves, and the heart that's been poisoned by them.

drill.q: Name the five signs that make a tachycardia (or a bradycardia) unstable.
drill.a: Hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure. Any one, caused by the rhythm → electricity (tachycardia) or atropine/pacing (bradycardia).

drill.q: Recurrent palpitations, normal BP, no chest pain or breathlessness, AF on ECG. Next step?
drill.a: Rate control (diltiazem or a β-blocker). Symptomatic is not unstable; only 30% avoided the shock (DocT).

drill.q: AHA 2025 synchronised cardioversion energies: AF, flutter, narrow SVT, monomorphic VT, polymorphic VT?
drill.a: AF ≥200 J, flutter 200 J, SVT 100 J, monomorphic VT 100 J; polymorphic VT = unsynchronised shock. Older keys give 100 J or 120–200 J for AF.

drill.q: AF 160/min, BP 84/50, crackles, duration unknown, not anticoagulated. Next step?
drill.a: Immediate synchronised cardioversion with heparin alongside. No TOE, no 3-week wait, no diltiazem or metoprolol.

drill.q: Stable AF >48 h: anticoagulation before and after cardioversion?
drill.a: 3 weeks before (or TOE to exclude LA clot), at least 4 weeks after whatever the stroke score (atrial stunning). ESC 2024 moves the line to 24 h.

drill.q: Stable regular narrow tachycardia 180/min: the order of treatment?
drill.a: Vagal manoeuvre (modified Valsalva) → adenosine 6 mg then 12 mg → β-blocker or CCB → synchronised cardioversion if all fail.

drill.q: Adenosine 6 mg slows the rate and shows saw-tooth waves at 300/min. Diagnosis?
drill.a: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction. Adenosine stops nodal circuits (AVNRT, AVRT) and only unmasks atrial rhythms.

drill.q: SVT in an asthmatic; and adenosine when the only access is an IJ line?
drill.a: Asthma: IV verapamil or diltiazem (7% right). Central line, transplant, dipyridamole, carbamazepine: 3 mg (Marrow); AHA 2025 says 1 mg may be adequate.

drill.q: Regular 180/min, inverted P in II, III, aVF hidden at the end of the QRS. Mechanism?
drill.a: Re-entry within the AV node (typical slow–fast AVNRT), not an accessory pathway (42% right). Commonest PSVT, young women.

drill.q: Carotid sinus massage: technique and contraindication?
drill.a: Supine, on ECG, one side only (right first), 5–10 s. Contraindicated with a carotid bruit or prior TIA/stroke. Modified Valsalva converts 43% vs 17% (REVERT).

drill.q: Which narrow-complex tachycardias are irregular, and does adenosine help?
drill.a: AF, flutter or atrial tachycardia with variable block, MAT. AVNRT and AVRT are always regular. Adenosine has no therapeutic role; give rate control.

drill.q: New AF with labile BP after surgery or in sepsis: which rate-control drug, and which to avoid?
drill.a: Esmolol (onset 2–3 min, t½ ~9 min) or IV amiodarone, after correcting K, Mg and volume. Avoid diltiazem and verapamil.

drill.q: AF with EF 30%, decompensated: what is avoided, what is banned, what is used?
drill.a: Avoid verapamil, diltiazem and IV β-blockers; dronedarone is contraindicated (ANDROMEDA, PALLAS). Use digoxin or amiodarone. Digoxin before dobutamine.

drill.q: Irregular wide tachycardia at 280/min with varying QRS shapes: diagnosis, banned drugs, treatment?
drill.a: Pre-excited AF (WPW). No adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blocker, digoxin or IV amiodarone. Procainamide or ibutilide; cardiovert if unstable.

drill.q: AF with rheumatic mitral stenosis or a mechanical valve: anticoagulant? And what did AFFIRM/RACE show?
drill.a: Warfarin, never a DOAC. Rate vs rhythm: no difference in mortality or stroke; rate control gave fewer rehospitalisations.

drill.q: CHA₂DS₂-VASc: which items score 2, and which factor is NOT in the score?
drill.a: Age ≥75 and prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism score 2. Male sex scores 0 (female 1). Anticoagulate at ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women.

drill.q: Stable monomorphic VT in decompensated heart failure: drug? And two drugs never given for a wide tachycardia?
drill.a: IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 min (procainamide if LV preserved: PROCAMIO). Never verapamil or diltiazem.

drill.q: The serious adverse effect of sotalol is due to what? When do you stop a procainamide infusion?
drill.a: QT prolongation and torsades from K⁺-channel (class III) block (NEET 2024). Procainamide: arrhythmia suppressed, hypotension, QRS +50%, or 17 mg/kg.

drill.q: Torsades on IV amiodarone: treatment, and what must not be given?
drill.a: Magnesium 2 g IV, overdrive pacing or isoprenaline if recurrent, stop the QT drug. Not amiodarone, procainamide or sotalol.

drill.q: Brugada: gene, ECG, when it kills, and the therapy after a survived arrest?
drill.a: SCN5A loss of function; coved ST ≥2 mm with a NEGATIVE T in V1–V2; rest, sleep, fever. ICD (class I); after arrhythmic syncope ICD is IIa; quinidine is only an adjunct (GT7 Q130).

drill.q: Primary-prevention ICD criteria, and what selects for CRT?
drill.a: EF ≤35%, NYHA II–III, ≥3 months of therapy, >40 days after MI. Arrest survivors with no reversible cause: ICD at any EF. CRT: LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms, not echo dyssynchrony.

drill.q: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II: the effect of atropine and exercise, and the infarct each goes with?
drill.a: Mobitz I (nodal, narrow, inferior MI): improves. Mobitz II (infranodal, wide, anterior MI): worsens or unchanged → pace.

drill.q: Bradycardia algorithm: atropine dose and maximum, then the infusion doses?
drill.a: Atropine 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg. Then TCP, or dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min, or adrenaline 2–10 mcg/min (not per kg). Then transvenous pacing.

drill.q: Unstable Mobitz II, BP 75/40: initial intervention? And bradycardia in a transplanted heart?
drill.a: Transcutaneous pacing first (43% right), then transvenous. Transplant: atropine fails; isoprenaline or adrenaline, or pace.

drill.q: Child, HR 46, poor perfusion despite good oxygenation and ventilation. Next step?
drill.a: Start CPR and give adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (22% right). Atropine 0.02 mg/kg only for vagal tone or primary AV block.

traps.trap: Stable AF with palpitations only: sedate and cardiovert at 100 J
traps.truth: None of the five instability signs, so rate control (diltiazem or a β-blocker).

traps.trap: Unstable wide-complex tachycardia: intubate first
traps.truth: Synchronised cardioversion. Marrow keyed the airway only because cardioversion was not offered.

traps.trap: Child's SVT recurs seconds after adenosine and is now unstable: more adenosine, diltiazem or amiodarone
traps.truth: Synchronised cardioversion 0.5–1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg. Verapamil and diltiazem cause collapse in infants.

traps.trap: Cardioversion is synchronised to the T wave (or P wave)
traps.truth: To the peak of the R wave; the T wave is what synchronisation avoids (R-on-T → VF).

traps.trap: Unstable AF: start at 100 J, or at 120–200 J
traps.truth: Cardioversion is the right choice, but AHA 2025 starts AF at ≥200 J (flutter 200 J). 100 J is for narrow SVT and monomorphic VT.
traps.asked: DocT QBank key (100 J), DocT CGT4 key (120–200 J)

traps.trap: Polymorphic VT with a pulse: synchronised 100 J, or magnesium
traps.truth: Immediate unsynchronised shock for sustained polymorphic VT (class 1). Magnesium is for recurrent torsades on a long QT.

traps.trap: Mandatory intubation or an arterial line before cardioversion
traps.truth: Sedate the awake patient where stability allows; nothing that delays the shock.

traps.trap: Anticoagulate for 2 or 3 weeks after cardioverting AF
traps.truth: 3 weeks before (or TOE); at least 4 weeks after, whatever the CHA₂DS₂-VASc.

traps.trap: Unstable AF of unknown duration: diltiazem or metoprolol first, or heparin and delayed cardioversion, or TOE first
traps.truth: Shock now with heparin alongside. Clot rules protect the stable patient from an elective procedure.

traps.trap: Amiodarone 150 mg for new post-operative AF with BP 73/34
traps.truth: Synchronised cardioversion; amiodarone is the stable patient's drug.

traps.trap: Stable SVT at 180/min: adenosine first
traps.truth: Vagal manoeuvre (modified Valsalva) first; adenosine when it fails.

traps.trap: AVRT is a cause of an irregular narrow-complex tachycardia
traps.truth: AVNRT and AVRT are always regular. Irregular = AF, flutter or atrial tachycardia with variable block, MAT.

traps.trap: Adenosine via an internal jugular line: still 6 mg
traps.truth: 3 mg (Marrow key) via a central line, after transplant, with dipyridamole or carbamazepine. AHA 2025: 1 mg may be adequate.

traps.trap: Asthmatic with SVT: adenosine
traps.truth: IV verapamil or diltiazem; adenosine can cause severe bronchospasm.

traps.trap: Inverted P in II, III, aVF at 180/min: re-entry via an accessory pathway
traps.truth: Typical AVNRT: re-entry within the AV node, P buried in or just after the QRS.

traps.trap: Modified Valsalva: take a deep breath before straining
traps.truth: A sustained strain at 40 mmHg for 15 s, then supine with legs raised.

traps.trap: HFrEF with AF 130/min and worsening dyspnoea: β-blocker
traps.truth: Disputed key. Decompensated HF: IV β-blockers and non-DHP CCBs are harm; amiodarone or digoxin plus a diuretic. Mark the β-blocker only if neither is offered.

traps.trap: Septic shock, new AF 140/min, BP 102/65: diltiazem or oral amiodarone
traps.truth: IV β-blocker (esmolol) is keyed; IV amiodarone is equally defensible. Diltiazem worsens hypotension; oral amiodarone is too slow.

traps.trap: Stable symptomatic AF: IV ibutilide
traps.truth: The stable irregular pathway is rate control. Ibutilide only when the stem asks to restore sinus rhythm in AF <48 h.

traps.trap: Verapamil is acceptable rate control with EF 30%; dronedarone is fine in severe HF
traps.truth: No verapamil or diltiazem below EF 40%. Dronedarone raises mortality in NYHA IV, recent decompensation and permanent AF.

traps.trap: Dabigatran is acceptable in rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF
traps.truth: Warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated in moderate–severe rheumatic MS and with mechanical valves.

traps.trap: Rhythm control reduces stroke compared with rate control
traps.truth: AFFIRM/RACE: no difference in mortality, stroke or quality of life; rate control → fewer rehospitalisations.

traps.trap: Male sex scores a point in CHA₂DS₂-VASc
traps.truth: Female sex scores 1, male 0. Two points: age ≥75 and prior stroke/TIA.

traps.trap: Stable monomorphic VT in a heart-failure patient: adenosine, verapamil or immediate cardioversion
traps.truth: IV amiodarone. Verapamil is harm, adenosine does not treat VT, electricity is for instability or drug failure.

traps.trap: Sotalol's main adverse effect is bradycardia or hypotension
traps.truth: QT prolongation and torsades from potassium-channel (class III) block.

traps.trap: WPW with AF: only verapamil is contraindicated
traps.truth: Every nodal blocker is harmful (adenosine, esmolol, digoxin, IV amiodarone too). Verapamil is the classic answer to mark.
traps.asked: DocT GT AIM1 Q36 / GT4 Q56, 45–54%

traps.trap: Delta wave and short PR: dual AV nodal pathway
traps.truth: An accessory AV pathway. Dual nodal pathways cause AVNRT with a normal ECG between attacks.

traps.trap: Brugada arrest survivor: quinidine (a drug) gives the greatest reduction in sudden death
traps.truth: ICD, class I, after a survived arrest (IIa after arrhythmic syncope). Quinidine is the adjunct if the ICD is refused or for recurrent shocks.

traps.trap: Positive T wave in V1–V2 as a Brugada feature
traps.truth: Type 1 is coved ST ≥2 mm with a NEGATIVE T. Saddle-back with a positive T is not diagnostic.

traps.trap: ICD for drug-induced polymorphic VT; amiodarone for torsades
traps.truth: Reversible cause: stop the drug, no ICD. Torsades: magnesium; amiodarone, procainamide and sotalol prolong the QT further.

traps.trap: Amiodarone for secondary prevention after a resuscitated arrest with EF 30%
traps.truth: ICD: beat amiodarone on mortality (AVID significant; CIDS and CASH concordant trends; pooled benefit), regardless of EF.

traps.trap: Echo mechanical dyssynchrony selects patients for CRT
traps.truth: QRS width does: LBBB with QRS ≥150 ms plus EF ≤35%.

traps.trap: Constant PP with a pause equal to two PP intervals: sinus arrest
traps.truth: SA exit block type II (pause is an exact multiple of the PP). A sinus pause has no fixed relation.

traps.trap: Anterior MI with second-degree block: Mobitz I, benign, give atropine
traps.truth: Wrong key. Anterior MI block is infranodal (LAD supplies His–Purkinje): no response to atropine, transvenous pacing.

traps.trap: Sleeping athlete with 2:1 block: His bundle or bundle branch
traps.truth: Vagal setting with a narrow QRS: AV node.

traps.trap: Asymptomatic first-degree AV block: admit or observe
traps.truth: Discharge; it needs no treatment.

traps.trap: Unstable Mobitz II: atropine first, or transvenous pacing as the initial step
traps.truth: Transcutaneous pacing at once as the bridge; atropine acts on the node and must not delay pacing.

traps.trap: After 3 mg of atropine, waiting for pacing: more atropine, norepinephrine or isoproterenol
traps.truth: Dopamine infusion (adrenaline if dopamine is not offered). 3 mg is full vagal blockade.

traps.trap: Atropine 0.5 mg as the adult dose
traps.truth: Pre-2020 AHA and current ERC dose. AHA 2020/2025: 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg. Pick 1 mg if offered.

traps.trap: Septic, HR 34, complete heart block, BP 80/50: permanent pacemaker
traps.truth: Atropine is keyed first (prepare TCP at once); a permanent pacemaker comes after stabilisation.

traps.trap: Adrenaline 2–10 mcg/kg/min for bradycardia
traps.truth: 2–10 mcg/min (not per kg). Dopamine is the one dosed per kg: 5–20 mcg/kg/min.

traps.trap: Electrical capture on the monitor confirms effective pacing; pace an asystolic arrest
traps.truth: Confirm mechanical capture with a femoral pulse or arterial trace. Routine pacing in established arrest is not recommended.

traps.trap: Bradycardia on metoprolol and digoxin: the β-blocker alone explains it
traps.truth: Digoxin is the synergistic culprit; both slow the AV node.

traps.trap: Atropine for bradycardia in a transplanted heart
traps.truth: Denervated: atropine, glycopyrrolate and ephedrine fail. Isoprenaline or adrenaline, or pacing.

traps.trap: Child with HR 46 and poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation: atropine or dopamine
traps.truth: Start CPR and give adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO.

mimics.pair: Symptomatic but stable vs unstable tachycardia
mimics.tell: Palpitations with a normal BP and mentation is stable; any of the five signs (hypotension, confusion, shock, chest pain, pulmonary oedema) is unstable.

mimics.pair: Cardioversion vs defibrillation
mimics.tell: An organised QRS to lock onto → synchronise on the R wave; VF or polymorphic VT → unsynchronised.

mimics.pair: Compensatory sinus tachycardia vs primary tachyarrhythmia
mimics.tell: Rate under about 150 with sepsis, bleeding or fever: treat the cause; a shock does nothing.

mimics.pair: Unstable AF vs stable AF of unknown duration
mimics.tell: Unstable: shock now with heparin. Stable: 3 weeks of anticoagulation or TOE first.

mimics.pair: AVNRT vs orthodromic AVRT
mimics.tell: AVNRT: P buried in the QRS (RP <70 ms), normal ECG between attacks. AVRT: P in the ST segment (RP >70 ms), delta wave between attacks if the pathway is manifest.

mimics.pair: Flutter 2:1 vs AVNRT
mimics.tell: Flutter: ventricular rate ~150; adenosine slows it and shows saw-tooth waves, then it returns. AVNRT terminates.

mimics.pair: Regular vs irregular narrow tachycardia
mimics.tell: Regular: nodal circuit, adenosine. Irregular: atrial source (AF, variable block, MAT), rate control.

mimics.pair: Compensated vs decompensated HFrEF with fast AF
mimics.tell: Compensated: β-blocker. Wet or hypotensive: digoxin or amiodarone plus a diuretic; no IV β-blocker.

mimics.pair: Valvular vs non-valvular AF
mimics.tell: Moderate–severe rheumatic MS or a mechanical valve: warfarin only. Bioprosthetic or other native valve disease: DOAC allowed.

mimics.pair: VT vs SVT with aberrancy
mimics.tell: AV dissociation (with fusion and capture beats) means VT; also QRS >160 ms, north-west axis, precordial concordance.

mimics.pair: Pre-excited AF vs VT (and vs polymorphic VT)
mimics.tell: Pre-excited AF is irregularly irregular with QRS width varying beat to beat, up to 300/min, no twisting; monomorphic VT is regular and uniform.

mimics.pair: Orthodromic AVRT vs pre-excited AF in WPW
mimics.tell: Regular and narrow: the node is in the circuit, adenosine allowed. Irregular and wide: no nodal blocker.

mimics.pair: Procainamide vs amiodarone for stable VT
mimics.tell: Preserved LV: procainamide (PROCAMIO). Poor LV or heart failure: amiodarone.

mimics.pair: Torsades (long QT) vs polymorphic VT with a normal QT
mimics.tell: Long QT: magnesium, pacing, stop QT drugs. Normal QT: ischaemia; amiodarone or β-blocker and angiography.

mimics.pair: Brugada vs CPVT
mimics.tell: Brugada: sodium channel, coved ST in V1–V2, dies at rest, in sleep or with fever. CPVT: RyR2, normal resting ECG, dies on exertion or emotion.

mimics.pair: Primary vs secondary prevention ICD
mimics.tell: Secondary: survived VF/VT with no reversible cause, any EF. Primary: no event, EF ≤35% on 3 months of therapy, >40 days after MI.

mimics.pair: Sinus bradycardia vs junctional rhythm
mimics.tell: Upright P before each QRS with a normal PR vs P inverted, absent or after a narrow QRS.

mimics.pair: SA exit block type II vs sinus pause
mimics.tell: Exit block: the pause is an exact multiple of the PP interval. Sinus pause: no fixed relation.

mimics.pair: Mobitz I vs Mobitz II
mimics.tell: Atropine or exercise improves Mobitz I (nodal) and worsens Mobitz II (infranodal).

mimics.pair: Mobitz II vs blocked premature atrial beats
mimics.tell: Blocked PACs come early and deform the T wave; in Mobitz II the non-conducted P is on time.

mimics.pair: Inferior-MI block vs anterior-MI block
mimics.tell: Inferior (RCA): nodal, narrow escape, atropine-responsive. Anterior (LAD): infranodal, wide escape, pace.

mimics.pair: Dopamine vs adrenaline infusion units in bradycardia
mimics.tell: Dopamine per kilogram (5–20 mcg/kg/min); adrenaline per minute (2–10 mcg/min).

mimics.pair: Pacing in bradycardia with a pulse vs in arrest
mimics.tell: A pulse: pacing helps. Established asystole or PEA: routine pacing gives no benefit.

mimics.pair: Adult vs child bradycardia with poor perfusion
mimics.tell: Adult: atropine, chronotrope, pacing. Child (hypoxic): oxygenate and ventilate; if HR still <60, CPR and adrenaline.

new_cards.q:
**CHA₂DS₂-VASc in non-valvular AF:**
a The items and their points
b The two items that score 2
c The threshold for anticoagulation
d What the score does NOT include
e The 2024 ESC change
a: **Anticoagulate at ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women**; consider at 1 (men) or 2 (women)
**Male sex scores 0.** Female sex is a risk modifier: it adds risk only with another factor
**ESC 2024: CHA₂DS₂-VA** (sex removed): anticoagulate at ≥2, consider at 1
Not used for valvular AF (moderate–severe rheumatic MS, mechanical valve): warfarin regardless of score
Trap: 'male sex' offered as a component of the score
new_cards.why: Marrow: 'AF stroke-risk score does NOT include which factor?' (male sex), and the item list with the ≥2 men / ≥3 women threshold. CAR-05 gives the anticoagulant and the cardioversion rule but not the score.

new_cards.topic: Vagal manoeuvres and adenosine: the fine print
new_cards.q:
**Breaking the AV node: give the fine print for:**
a The modified Valsalva: how, and its result (REVERT)
b Carotid sinus massage: how
c Its contraindications
d When to reduce the first dose of adenosine
e What blunts adenosine
a: **Modified Valsalva:** strain at **40 mmHg for 15 s** semi-recumbent, then **lie flat with legs raised 45° for 15 s**; converts **43% vs 17%** for the standard manoeuvre (REVERT)
It is a sustained strain, **not** a deep breath in
**Carotid sinus massage:** supine, continuous ECG, **ONE side only** (right first), **5–10 s**; never bilateral
**Contraindicated:** **carotid bruit**, prior TIA or stroke (plaque embolism)

**Reduce adenosine to 3 mg** (Marrow key): **central line**, **heart transplant** (denervated, supersensitive), **dipyridamole**, **carbamazepine**. AHA 2025: 1 mg may be adequate via a central line or after transplant
**Blunted by theophylline and caffeine** (adenosine-receptor antagonists): larger doses may be needed
Trap: 'still 6 mg' through an internal jugular line
new_cards.why: Marrow (adenosine via an IJ line = 3 mg; potentiators and antagonists; 'deep breath before straining' as the false statement), DocT GT (carotid bruit as the contraindication to carotid sinus massage), DocT GT + Marrow (REVERT technique). ACLS-31 and CAR-02 give only 6 mg then 12 mg and 'vagal manoeuvres'.

card_flags.issue: Part b's banned list for pre-excited AF (adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, β-blockers, digoxin) omits IV amiodarone, which ACC/AHA 2023 and AHA 2025 class as harm (COR 3) and which ACLS-33 already lists. Suggest adding it.

Part d says 'ICD for survivors'. Suggest making it explicit: ICD is class I after a survived arrest (GT7 Q130, missed) and is also indicated after arrhythmic syncope (Marrow); quinidine only if the ICD is refused or for recurrent shocks. Part a calls magnesium the drug of choice; AHA 2025 grades it COR 2b (may be considered) for recurrent torsades. The NEET answer is unchanged.

Part b uses the 48-hour line (exam answer; ACC/AHA 2023). ESC 2024 moved it to 24 hours and replaced CHA₂DS₂-VASc with CHA₂DS₂-VA. Card is not wrong for NEET; consider a one-line note. The score itself was on no card (now V12-015).

The card lists 100 J for narrow-complex tachycardia and monomorphic VT as '2025 energies'. The AHA 2025 guideline text gives a figure only for AF (≥200 J, 2a) and flutter (200 J, 2b); the 100 J values come from the algorithm chart. Consider wording 'AF ≥200 J' (the card says 200 J).

Card has no reduced-dose line. The pack's two explanations disagree: ACLS-31 says 3 mg via a central line or after transplant (Marrow key); CAR-02 says AHA 2025 '1 mg may be adequate'. Both are true (checked against the AHA 2025 Part 9 text); taught as 3 mg for the exam, 1 mg per AHA 2025. Covered by new card V12-016.

Withdrawn by the checker. The pack's 'post-ROSC adrenaline 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min' matches the AHA 2015/2020 post-cardiac-arrest algorithm (epinephrine 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min, norepinephrine 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min), so it is not an error. Leaving it out of the lesson is still right: the bradycardia dose is 2–10 mcg/min.

SA exit block (type I vs type II vs sinus pause) was asked in a DocT GT (75%) and is on no card. Section P12-505 is already at 8 steps, so I taught it inside this lesson with its own takeaway and did not add a card. Suggest a V12 card or an added line if the section limit allows.
